claims.source: SST cells exhibit reciprocal inhibitory connections with PV cells and also VIP cells in each layer, which brings these cell pairs in competition with each other (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the connectivity structure in the model shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Input to VIP or PV cells can suppress SST activity.
claims.source: To verify this hypothesis, we first tested whether input to VIP or PV cells can suppress SST activity.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the model simulations.

claims.claim: As G increased, the responses of SST cells became more switch like with sigmoidal curves in both layers, a hallmark of an ultrasensitive switch in many biological systems.
claims.source: Second, as G increased, the responses of SST cells became more switch like with sigmoidal curves in both layers, a hallmark of an ultrasensitive switch in many biological systems (Ferrell and Ha, 2014; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 3A, with reference to biological systems.

claims.claim: A similar sigmoidal decrease in SST firing rates with initial PYR disinhibition followed by inhibition was observed in both layers when only PV cells were driven.
claims.source: A similar sigmoidal decrease in SST firing rates with initial PYR disinhibition followed by inhibition was observed in both layers when only PV cells were driven (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claims.claim: Hysteresis appeared at sufficiently high G values, as visible by the appearance of noncongruent response curves for the up and down direction in all cell types of both layers for VIP and PV input.
claims.source: We found that hysteresis appeared at sufficiently high G values, as visible by the appearance of noncongruent response curves for the up and down direction in all cell types of both layers for VIP (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) and PV input (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claims.claim: Inhibition-based ultrasensitivity and hysteresis commonly require strong inhibitory interactions between the components of the system.
claims.source: Inhibition-based ultrasensitivity and hysteresis commonly require strong inhibitory interactions between the components of the system (Ferrell, 2002).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ferrell, 2002.

claims.claim: Selectively increasing the mutual inhibitory connections between SST <> VIP and SST <> PV cells was sufficient for ultrasensitivity and hysteresis to appear in the microcircuit.
claims.source: Indeed, selectively increasing these weights was sufficient for ultrasensitivity and hysteresis to appear in the microcircuit (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in a figure supplement.

claims.claim: Both nH and h increased monotonically with G when either VIP cells or PV cells were stimulated.
claims.source: We found that both nH and h increased monotonically with G when either VIP cells (Figure 4A) or PV cells (Figure 4B) were stimulated.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: The addition of noise does not change the switching dynamics results.
claims.source: We found that the addition of noise does not change the results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness testing shown in a figure supplement.

claims.claim: The jitter in the connection weights changed the slope of the SST response curves.
claims.source: The jitter in the connection weights indeed changed the slope of the SST response curves (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), which resulted in a large variety of Hill coefficient values (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness testing shown in figure supplements.

claims.claim: Both input to VIP and PV cells strongly increased the frequency of the dominant oscillation in superficial and deep layers, whereas the power of the oscillation peak generally decreased.
claims.source: Both input to VIP and PV cells strongly increased the frequency of the dominant oscillation in superficial and deep layers, whereas the power of the oscillation peak generally decreased (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: A marked transition between a slow and fast oscillation state was still visible, even when the time constant across all neurons was the same.
claims.source: Remarkably, a marked transition between a slow and fast oscillation state was still visible, even when the time constant across all neurons was the same.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claims.claim: Driving SST cells resulted in a monotonic decay of activity of all other cell types in both layers for different values of G, in line with several experimental studies.
claims.source: Driving SST cells resulted in a monotonic decay of activity of all other cell types in both layers for different values of G (Figure 6B), in line with several experimental studies (Chen, 2017; Dipoppa et al., 2018; Adesnik et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6B that is consistent with experimental studies cited.

claims.claim: Stimulation of SST cells reduced the frequency of oscillations.
claims.source: Stimulation of SST cells also reduced the frequency of oscillations (Figure 6C–E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6C-E.

claims.claim: As input to SST cells increased, the power of oscillations initially increased and subsequently decreased once PV cells were strongly suppressed.
claims.source: However, as we increased the input to SST cells the power of oscillations initially increased and subsequently decreased once PV cells were strongly suppressed.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: This finding replicates experimental results, in which stronger surround suppression is followed by a sudden transition from high frequency (gamma range) to lower frequency oscillations (high beta, low gamma range) and a concomitant increase in oscillatory power in mouse V1.
claims.source: This finding replicates experimental results, in which stronger surround suppression is followed by a sudden transition from high frequency (gamma range) to lower frequency oscillations (high beta, low gamma range) and a concomitant increase in oscillatory power in mouse V1 (Chen, 2017; Veit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement connects the model finding to experimental results cited.

claims.claim: Stimulation of PYR cells strongly increased SST activity in both layers.
claims.source: In this case, PYR input strongly increased SST activity (Figure 7A) (and to a lesser extent PV rates, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) in both layers, while VIP cells were suppressed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claims.claim: Sufficiently high PYR input and G value caused a jump back to higher SST activity in both layers when VIP cells received a constant external input.
claims.source: In this case, sufficiently high PYR input and G value caused a jump back to higher SST activity in both layers (Figure 7B) with a sudden suppression of PV and VIP activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in figures.

claims.claim: These findings are consistent with recent optogenetic experiments in which strong PYR drive was associated with high SST activity and comparatively low PV rates.
claims.source: These findings are consistent with recent optogenetic experiments in which strong PYR drive was associated with high SST activity and comparatively low PV rates (Hakim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claims.claim: The switching dynamics was preserved even in the absence of recurrent excitation, highlighting the fact that the switch is implemented by interactions among the three inhibitory neurons types.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the switching dynamics was preserved even in the absence of recurrent excitation, highlighting the fact that the switch is implemented by interactions among the three inhibitory neurons types.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with manipulated recurrent excitation.

claims.claim: Input to VIP cells in the superficial layer showed a disinhibitory PYR rate increase in the deep layer, which was mainly due to a translaminar reduction of SST activity rather than a direct drive from superficial to deep PYR cells.
claims.source: When the circuit displayed high SST activity, input to VIP cells in the superficial layer showed a disinhibitory PYR rate increase in the deep layer, which was mainly due to a translaminar reduction of SST activity rather than a direct drive from superficial to deep PYR cells (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Transitions between disinhibited and inhibited states triggered in one layer can propagate to the opposite layer and this interlayer interaction is primarily governed by translaminar SST connections.
claims.source: In summary, these results demonstrate that transitions between disinhibited and inhibited states triggered in one layer can propagate to the opposite layer and this interlayer interaction is primarily governed by translaminar SST connections.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations with translaminar connection manipulations.

claims.claim: L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers.
claims.source: The extent of this drive through PYR cells is cell specific, as for instance L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers (Adesnik et al., 2012), while feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells (Zhang et al., 2014; Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Adesnik et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells.
claims.source: The extent of this drive through PYR cells is cell specific, as for instance L4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers (Adesnik et al., 2012), while feedback input from the anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells (Zhang et al., 2014; Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: For small G values all cell types enhanced their activity for both feedforward and feedback types of drive, while there was a gradual suppression of SST cells for larger values.
claims.source: For small G values all cell types enhanced their activity for both types of drive, while we found a gradual suppression of SST cells for larger values (Figure 9B, C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 9B and 9C.

claims.claim: In both feedforward and feedback input models, a suppression of the spontaneous low-frequency oscillation and a corresponding enhancement of higher frequency oscillations was observed due to strong PV and VIP activation.
claims.source: In both input models we observed a suppression of the spontaneous low-frequency oscillation and a corresponding enhancement of higher frequency oscillations due to strong PV and VIP activation (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: These results are consistent with the experimental literature, which reported alpha oscillation suppression and gamma oscillation enhancement upon both visual stimulation and feedback associated visual attention.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the experimental literature, which reported alpha oscillation suppression and gamma oscillation enhancement upon both visual stimulation (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014) and feedback associated visual attention (Klimesch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claims.claim: There is a strong asymmetry between recurrent connections among PV and SST cells: connections between PV cells in each layer are the strongest within the entire matrix, while recurrent connections among SST cells are entirely absent.
claims.source: To this end, we examined the mouse V1 connectivity matrix and found that there is a strong asymmetry between recurrent connections among PV and SST cells. While connections between PV cells in each layer are the strongest within the entire matrix, recurrent connections among SST cells are entirely absent (Figure 10A, Supplementary file 1d).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the connectivity matrix shown in Figure 10A and Supplementary file 1d.

claims.claim: The strong self-inhibition of PV cells effectively reduces their inhibitory effect on PYR cells, while SST cells can elicit comparatively stronger inhibition on PYR cells due to the absence of self-inhibition.
claims.source: Thus, we hypothesized that the strong self-inhibition of PV cells effectively reduces their inhibitory effect on PYR cells, while SST cells can elicit comparatively stronger inhibition on PYR cells due to the absence of self-inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the connectivity structure.

claims.claim: Exchanging the recurrent connections between PV and SST cells inverted their role in microcircuit state switching.
claims.source: If this was true, exchanging the recurrent connections, that is removing PV self-connections and add them to SST cells may invert their role in microcircuit state switching (Figure 10A). In simulations with the inverted connectivity scheme we found that input to SST cells indeed created a disinhibition peak in the PYR cell response (Figure 10B, left), similar to VIP input in the original connectivity scheme (Figure 3A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), while PV and VIP cells showed a monotonic suppression (Figure 10B, right, Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with modified connectivity shown in figures.

claims.claim: Inhibitory state-dependent alterations in excitation–inhibition balance, which are at the core of the switching properties of the microcircuit, are due to large differences in PV and SST self-connectivity.
claims.source: These results indeed suggest that inhibitory state-dependent alterations in excitation–inhibition balance, which are at the core of the switching properties of the microcircuit, are due to large differences in PV and SST self-connectivity (Figure 10E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations with modified connectivity.

claims.claim: Superficial and deep layers of the mouse V1 microcircuit are endowed with two switch mechanisms that can toggle the pyramidal cells between high (disinhibited) and low activity states (inhibited) across superficial and deep layers.
claims.source: In this study, we showed that superficial and deep layers of the mouse V1 microcircuit are endowed with two switch mechanisms that can toggle the pyramidal cells (output of the microcircuit) between high (disinhibited) and low activity states (inhibited) across superficial and deep layers (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study shown in Figure 10F.

claims.claim: The underlying switching mechanics are realized by the interactions among the three interneuron types (PV, SST, and VIP), which compete for inhibitory influence on pyramidal cells.
claims.source: The underlying switching mechanics are realized by the interactions among the three interneuron types (PV, SST, and VIP), which compete for inhibitory influence on pyramidal cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claims.claim: In the inhibited state, SST cells dominate inhibition which serve as 'master regulators' by strongly connecting and inhibiting activity of pyramidal cells and other interneurons in the circuit.
claims.source: In the inhibited state, SST cells dominate inhibition which serve as 'master regulators' by strongly connecting and inhibiting activity of pyramidal cells and other interneurons in the circuit (Jiang et al., 2015; Chen, 2017; Fino and Yuste, 2011; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Naka et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: In the disinhibited state, excitation is mainly balanced by PV cells and to a lesser extent by VIP neurons, whereas SST activity is reduced.
claims.source: In the disinhibited state, excitation is mainly balanced by PV cells (Ferguson and Gao, 2018) and to a lesser extent by VIP neurons (Garcia-Junco-Clemente et al., 2017), whereas SST activity is reduced.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Disinhibition through SST suppression was previously shown experimentally and theoretically.
claims.source: While disinhibition through SST suppression was previously shown experimentally and theoretically (Pi et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2016; Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019; Wang and Yang, 2018), the question remains why SST cells provide more inhibition than PV or VIP cells, even though the weights of the PV to PYR connections by far outweigh SST to PYR connections (Supplementary file 1d).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claims.claim: Similar to previous simulations of anatomically simplified neuronal networks, self-inhibition of PV cells reduced their impact on PYR cells and enhanced PYR rates.
claims.source: Similar to previous simulations of anatomically simplified neuronal networks (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019), we found that a key to this inhibitory asymmetry lies in the degree to which PV and SST cells are connected among themselves. While SST cells lack mutual connectivity, PV cells have strong mutual connectivity (that may also be reinforced by gap junctions Pfeffer et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015; Bartos et al., 2007). In our rate model, self-inhibition of PV cells reduced their impact on PYR cells and enhanced PYR rates.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with previous simulations cited.

claims.claim: A similar effect was found in spiking network models, where PV interactions enhanced PYR rates and synchrony.
claims.source: We note that a similar effect was found in spiking network models, where PV interactions enhanced PYR rates and synchrony (Hahn et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a spiking network model study.

claims.claim: The switching mechanism emerges as a consequence of two mutual inhibitory connection motifs from SST to PV and VIP, and PV/VIP to SST neurons, in both layers.
claims.source: The switching mechanism emerges as a consequence of two mutual inhibitory connection motifs that is from SST to PV and VIP, and PV/VIP to SST neurons, in both layers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model about the mechanism of switching.

claims.claim: The nature of the switch depended on the mutual inhibitory connectivity strength, rendering the state transition purely ultrasensitive with sigmoidal input–output curves for weaker weights or bistable with hysteresis and memory for stronger weights.
claims.source: The nature of this switch depended on the mutual inhibitory connectivity strength, rendering the state transition purely ultrasensitive with sigmoidal input–output curves for weaker weights or bistable with hysteresis and memory for stronger weights, consistent with recent observations made in simplified inhibitory neuronal networks (Hertäg and Sprekeler, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with previous observations cited.

claims.claim: Switching based on double negative feedback has been conserved during evolution in many biological systems.
claims.source: Switching based on double negative feedback has been conserved during evolution in many biological systems (Ferrell and Ha, 2014; Ferrell, 2002; Tyson et al., 2003) and we found that it may also be a hallmark of cortical microcircuits.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on biological systems.

claims.claim: The two ways to control the switch differ in their sensitivity, with VIP cells requiring considerably less input to control SST activity and flip the circuit to the disinhibited state in both layers than PV cells.
claims.source: Notably, the two ways to control the switch differ in their sensitivity, with VIP cells requiring considerably less input to control SST activity and flip the circuit to the disinhibited state in both layers than PV cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: PV cells seem to be more specialized in keeping the excitation–inhibition balance at sufficiently high levels, whereas VIP cells play more a switching role, even though both cell types can assume both functions.
claims.source: Thus, PV cells seem to be more specialized in keeping the excitation–inhibition balance at sufficiently high levels, whereas VIP cells play more a switching role, even though both cell types can assume both functions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claims.claim: Each layer can transmit its state change to the other through translaminar connectivity, and effectively synchronize inhibited or disinhibited states across the whole microcircuit.
claims.source: The switching circuitry of the microcircuit can not only be activated by simultaneous input to superficial and deep layers, but each layer can transmit its state change to the other through translaminar connectivity, and effectively synchronize inhibited or disinhibited states across the whole microcircuit.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: The two-layer microcircuit as a whole can act as a switch, whose state may be used to guide activity flow of pyramidal cells in the feedforward (via L2/3) and feedback direction (L5).
claims.source: These results suggest that the two-layer microcircuit as a whole can act as a switch, whose state may be used to guide activity flow of pyramidal cells in the feedforward (via L2/3) and feedback direction (L5) (Markov et al., 2014b; Markov et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations.

claims.claim: The presence of bistability based on mutual inhibitory connection motifs provides an alternative to the dominant view that persistent transitions between low and high firing rate states across the brain are primarily based on local or interareal recurrent connectivity between excitatory neurons.
claims.source: The presence of bistability based on mutual inhibitory connection motifs also provides an alternative to the dominant view that persistent transitions between low and high firing rate states across the brain (Christophel et al., 2017), which underlie working memory required for attention (Ardid et al., 2014), consciousness (Dehaene et al., 2014; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; van Vugt et al., 2018), and language processing (Kunze et al., 2017; Nelson et al., 2017; Pallier et al., 2011), are primarily based on local (Compte et al., 2000) or interareal (Dehaene et al., 2014; van Vugt et al., 2018) recurrent connectivity between excitatory neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on persistent states.

claims.claim: Bistability is controlled by properties of local inhibitory connectivity, opening up the possibility that anatomical heterogeneity and gradients across the brain may reflect the presence of bistable switches in some brain areas and ultrasensitive switches without memory in other regions.
claims.source: In our study, bistability is controlled by properties of local inhibitory connectivity, opening up the possibility that anatomical heterogeneity and gradients across the brain may reflect the presence of bistable switches in some brain areas and ultrasensitive switches without memory in other regions (Kim et al., 2017; Fulcher et al., 2019; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on brain heterogeneity.

claims.claim: Two negative feedback loops between pyramidal cells and interneurons endow both deep and superficial layers with an intrinsic oscillation.
claims.source: Two negative feedback loops between pyramidal cells and interneurons endow both deep and superficial layers with an intrinsic oscillation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model about the mechanism of oscillations.

claims.claim: Consistent with experiments and models, PV cells drive high frequencies ('gamma range'), whereas SST cells prefer lower frequencies ('beta range').
claims.source: Consistent with experiments and models, PV cells drive high frequencies ('gamma range'), whereas SST cells prefer lower frequencies ('beta range') (Cardin et al., 2009; Chen, 2017; Lee, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with experiments and models cited.

claims.claim: During the inhibited switch state the dominating SST cells impose a slower frequency on PYR cells as compared to the PV dominated disinhibition state with high frequencies.
claims.source: Accordingly, during the inhibited switch state the dominating SST cells impose a slower frequency on PYR cells as compared to the PV dominated disinhibition state with high frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: VIP cells had little influence on oscillation frequency.
claims.source: VIP cells had little influence on oscillation frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: The switch in frequency is already shaped by the connectivity pattern of the circuit and is only partly modified by intrinsic neuronal properties such as differing time constants.
claims.source: An interesting finding of our study is that this switch in frequency is already shaped by the connectivity pattern of the circuit and is only partly modified by intrinsic neuronal properties such as differing time constants.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claims.claim: In the absence of noise and oscillations, the ability of the network to change its frequency is not dependent on the exact time constant of neuron populations suggesting that the switch is already engrained in the connectivity.
claims.source: Note also that in the absence of noise and oscillations, the ability of the network to change its frequency is not dependent on the exact time constant of neuron populations suggesting that the switch is already engrained in the connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: Neuron population time constants determine the amount of change in the oscillation frequency as the network goes from SST to PV mode.
claims.source: Neuron population time constants, however, do determine the amount of change in the oscillation frequency as the network goes from SST to PV mode.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with varied time constants.

claims.claim: This result provides a potential explanation for a longstanding question of what determines the oscillation frequency in neuronal circuits.
claims.source: This result thus provides a potential explanation for a longstanding question of what determines the oscillation frequency in neuronal circuits (Brunel and Wang, 2003; Jia et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations to studies on oscillation frequency.

claims.claim: This finding is in contrast to previous modeling efforts which introduced slow and high frequencies by endowing interneurons with different time constants.
claims.source: This finding is in contrast to previous modeling efforts which introduced slow and high frequencies by endowing interneurons with different time constants (Hyafil et al., 2015; Mejias et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement contrasts the current findings with previous modeling approaches cited.

claims.claim: Animal experiments have revealed that the power of high-frequency oscillations was stronger in the superficial layer, while slower oscillation had more power in the deep layers.
claims.source: Animal experiments have revealed that the power of high-frequency oscillations was stronger in the superficial layer, while slower oscillation had more power in the deep layers (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Haegens, 2015; Buffalo et al., 2011; Bonaiuto et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The emergence of differences in oscillations in deep and superficial layers crucially depends on specific anatomical connections.
claims.source: Based on our results we argue that the emergence of such differences in oscillations in deep and superficial layers crucially depends on specific anatomical connections (see Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Visual stimulation mediated by feedforward connections and visual attention mediated by feedback connections suppress slow oscillations (alpha band) and enhance fast oscillations in the gamma band.
claims.source: Moreover, our results also replicate experimental findings which have shown that visual stimulation mediated by feedforward connections and visual attention mediated by feedback connections suppress slow oscillations (alpha band) and enhance fast oscillations in the gamma band (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Klimesch, 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement connects the model findings to experimental results cited.

claims.claim: The results suggest an alternative, anatomically based taxonomy for oscillations, dividing them into competing SST- (low frequency) and PV-driven rhythms (high frequency).
claims.source: Thus, our results also suggest an alternative, anatomically based taxonomy for oscillations, dividing them into competing SST- (low frequency) and PV-driven rhythms (high frequency).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claims.claim: During the transition between (PV or SST dominated) switch states the oscillation frequency and power behave asymmetrically, that is an increase in frequency is accompanied by a decrease in power.
claims.source: Notably, during the transition between (PV or SST dominated) switch states the oscillation frequency and power behave asymmetrically, that is an increase in frequency is accompanied by a decrease in power.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claims.claim: When PV or SST cells are strongly suppressed or silenced, frequency and power change symmetrically.
claims.source: However, when PV or SST cells are strongly suppressed or silenced, frequency and power change symmetrically.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with cell silencing.

claims.claim: A decrease in frequency and increase in power is found in recent experiments in monkeys and mice, in which small stimuli trigger a high-frequency oscillation (~60 Hz) that is replaced by a lower frequency (~30 Hz) in the presence of larger stimuli.
claims.source: A decrease in frequency and increase in power is also found in recent experiments in monkeys and mice, in which small stimuli trigger a high-frequency oscillation (~60 Hz) that is replaced by a lower frequency (~30 Hz) in the presence of larger stimuli (Chen, 2017; Veit et al., 2017; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Anatomical studies show that surround suppression effect is presumably mediated by lateral excitatory input from the surround to SST neurons in the center.
claims.source: Anatomical studies show that this surround suppression effect is presumably mediated by lateral excitatory input from the surround to SST neurons in the center (Adesnik et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claims.claim: The model suggests that the surround switches the microcircuit from a PV/VIP dominated state with a high frequency, putatively mediated by stimulus triggered feedforward and feedback drive, to a more inhibited state caused by enhanced lateral drive to SST cells.
claims.source: Our model suggests that the surround switches the microcircuit from a PV/VIP dominated state with a high frequency, putatively mediated by stimulus triggered feedforward and feedback drive (Zhang et al., 2014; Gonchar and Burkhalter, 2003), to a more inhibited state caused by enhanced lateral drive to SST cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model supported by citations.

claims.claim: Experiments have also reported the inverse case with an increase in oscillation frequency and decrease in power after enhancing visual stimulus contrast.
claims.source: We note that experiments have also reported the inverse case with an increase in oscillation frequency and decrease in power after enhancing visual stimulus contrast (Ray and Maunsell, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: The coupling parameter G can be related to the overall cell count in the studied circuits.
claims.source: The switching properties in the model depend on the coupling parameter G, which scales the overall connectivity between neurons of the circuit. This parameter has been previously used to study whole-brain models of cortical dynamics (Deco et al., 2013) and can be related to the overall cell count in the studied circuits.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Feedforward and feedback input lead to suppression of SST and PYR activity for sufficiently high G values, which is inconsistent with recent experimental results in mouse V1, where the rate of all cell types increased after visual stimulation.
claims.source: We found that feedforward and feedback input lead to suppression of SST and PYR activity for sufficiently high G values. This is inconsistent with recent experimental results in mouse V1, where the rate of all cell types increased after visual stimulation (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model that is inconsistent with experimental results cited.

claims.claim: Smaller values of G may be biologically more realistic for mouse V1.
claims.source: This suggests that smaller values of G may be biologically more realistic for mouse V1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of model results with experimental data.

claims.claim: The connectivity matrix used in the model is based on the detailed anatomical study of Jiang et al., 2015, which did not capture layers 4 and 6 of mouse V1.
claims.source: The connectivity matrix used in the model is based on the detailed anatomical study of Jiang et al., 2015, which did not capture layers 4 and 6 of mouse V1.
claims.evidence: This describes a limitation of the model based on the source of connectivity data.

claims.claim: There is limited anatomical knowledge about the cell-specific connectivity within layers 4 and 6 and their connections to other layers in the microcircuit.
claims.source: There exist a number of studies which have charted the different morphological and biochemical cell types in these two layers, which can also be divided into PV, SST, and VIP classes similar to layers 2/3 and 5 in the present study (Scala et al., 2019; Frandolig et al., 2019; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Ding et al., 2021). However, there is limited anatomical knowledge about the cell-specific connectivity within each layer and their connections to other layers in the microcircuit.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on cell types and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claims.claim: The disinhibited state of the switch naturally entails the risk of runaway excitation.
claims.source: The disinhibited state of the switch naturally entails the risk of runaway excitation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the potential consequences of the disinhibited state.

claims.claim: The microcircuit contains supplementary homeostatic mechanisms that keep disinhibition within healthy boundaries.
claims.source: Our results provide evidence that the microcircuit contains supplementary homeostatic mechanisms that keep disinhibition within healthy boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model simulations.

claims.claim: When the circuit is disinhibited and SST activity suppressed, strong drive to pyramidal cell can cause a sudden reversal of SST neurons to a high firing rate state and thereby restore a more inhibited state in the microcircuit.
claims.source: When the circuit is disinhibited and SST activity suppressed, strong drive to pyramidal cell can cause a sudden reversal of SST neurons to a high firing rate state and thereby restore a more inhibited state in the microcircuit.

claims.claim: Different interneurons were labeled as PV cells (layer 2/3: basket cells and chandelier cells; layer 5: shrub cells and horizontally elongated cells), SST cells (layers 2/3 and 5: Martinotti cells), and VIP cells (only layer 2/3: bitufted cells and bipolar cells) based on their genetic makeup.
claims.source: Finally, based on their genetic makeup, different interneurons were labeled as PV cells (layer 2/3: basket cells and chandelier cells; layer 5: shrub cells and horizontally elongated cells), SST cells (layers 2/3 and 5: Martinotti cells), and VIP cells (only layer 2/3: bitufted cells and bipolar cells).
claims.evidence: This describes the classification of interneurons used in the model.

claims.claim: A single connectivity matrix (C) was created by element-wise multiplication of EPSP/IPSP strength (i.e., mean amplitude) and connection probability matrices.
claims.source: To convert the original connectivity data (see Supplementary file 1a for the connection probability matrix and Supplementary file 1b for the weight [EPSP/IPSP] matrix) into a format suited for a computational model, we performed several manipulations. First, restricting our analysis to pyramidal cells and three major interneurons types (PV, SST, and VIP), we created a single connectivity matrix (C) by element-wise multiplication of EPSP/IPSP strength (i.e., mean amplitude) and connection probability matrices.

claims.claim: VIP neurons were divided into VIPsup and VIPdeep cell types based on their preferential targeting of other neurons in L2/3 or L5, even though both types were anatomically located in the superficial layer.
claims.source: After inspection of the connectivity matrix, we noticed that out of the two existing VIP cell types, one VIP cell type preferentially targeted other neurons in L2/3 (bitufted cells), whereas the other only innervated L5 (bipolar cells). Based on this observation, we divided VIP neurons into VIPsup and VIPdeep cell types, even though both types were anatomically located in the superficial layer.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the model based on connectivity patterns.

claims.claim: All inhibitory weights in the matrix were scaled down by a factor of 0.2 to account for the roughly five times more pyramidal neurons in a microcircuit than interneurons.
claims.source: Thus, we had four neuron types in both deep and superficial layers. Instead of modeling populations of neurons with N cells for each class, we modeled each cell population using a single firing rate-based neuron. However, we adapted the connectivity weights according to their relative prevalence, which is computationally less expensive. To this end, we first followed the general rule that there are roughly five times more pyramidal neurons in a microcircuit than interneurons. Therefore, all inhibitory weights in the matrix were scaled down by a factor of 0.2.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological step in creating the model based on known cell prevalence.

claims.claim: The weights of each interneuron type were multiplied with its relative prevalence.

results.result: The mouse V1 microcircuit implements two ultrasensitive and bistable switches based on mutual inhibitory connectivity between SST, PV, and VIP interneurons that toggle pyramidal neurons between inhibited and disinhibited states.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C13, C15, C62, C63, and C69 collectively describe the core switching mechanism. The computational model demonstrates that mutual inhibitory motifs between SST↔PV and SST↔VIP create ultrasensitive switches (C32, C36, C37) with sigmoidal response curves and hysteresis at high coupling strengths (C34, C70). The model shows robustness to noise (C38) and connectivity variations (C39), supporting the biological plausibility of this mechanism.

results.result: State transitions triggered in one cortical layer propagate to the other layer through translaminar SST connections, synchronizing inhibited or disinhibited states across the microcircuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C51, C52, and C74 describe translaminar propagation of circuit states. The model demonstrates that VIP or PV input to one layer causes disinhibition in the opposite layer primarily through translaminar SST connections (C51, Figure 8). Selective removal of translaminar connections in the model abolishes this effect, confirming the mechanism. This is a well-controlled computational experiment with clear causal manipulation.

results.result: Inhibited and disinhibited states are characterized by low-frequency (beta) and high-frequency (gamma) oscillations respectively, with asymmetric changes in frequency and power during state transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C16, C79, C80, and C91 describe oscillatory properties of circuit states. The model shows SST-dominated states produce beta oscillations (~15-40 Hz) while PV-dominated states produce gamma oscillations (~60-110 Hz) (C26, C27, C28). During transitions, frequency and power change asymmetrically—frequency increases while power decreases (C40, C91). This asymmetry is abolished when PV or SST cells are silenced (C92, C109), providing internal validation. Results match experimental observations (C16, C24, C46).

results.result: The differential inhibitory impact of PV versus SST cells on pyramidal neurons is explained by strong recurrent inhibition among PV cells versus absent recurrent connections among SST cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 and C67 explain the mechanistic basis for differential inhibition. The model identifies strong PV-PV connections and absent SST-SST connections in the connectivity matrix (C58). When these connections are experimentally swapped in the model, the roles of PV and SST cells invert (C60), with SST input now causing disinhibition. This computational manipulation provides strong causal evidence for the proposed mechanism and is consistent with prior simplified models (C67).

results.result: The switches exhibit ultrasensitivity with sigmoidal response curves at moderate coupling strengths and bistability with hysteresis at high coupling strengths, controlled by mutual inhibitory connection strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C34, C36, C37, and C70 characterize the switching dynamics. The model demonstrates sigmoidal SST response curves with increasing Hill coefficients (nH) as coupling parameter G increases (C32, C37, Figure 3A, 4A-B). Hysteresis appears at sufficiently high G values (C34, Figure 3C-D). Selectively increasing mutual inhibitory weights between SST↔VIP and SST↔PV is sufficient to produce ultrasensitivity and hysteresis (C36), confirming the mechanism. The quantitative characterization using Hill coefficients and hysteresis area provides rigorous evidence.

results.result: VIP cells require less input than PV cells to suppress SST activity and switch the circuit to the disinhibited state, suggesting VIP cells are specialized for switching while PV cells maintain excitation-inhibition balance.
results.evaluation: Claims C72 and C73 describe differential sensitivity of the two switches. The model shows VIP-mediated switching occurs at lower G values than PV-mediated switching (Figure 4C-D), and VIP input requires less current to suppress SST cells. This is supported by quantitative analysis of Hill coefficients and hysteresis onset across different G values. The functional interpretation (C73) is a reasonable inference from the model behavior.

results.result: The frequency switch between slow and fast oscillations is primarily determined by the connectivity pattern rather than intrinsic neuronal time constants, though time constants modulate the magnitude of frequency changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 and C41 describe the basis of oscillation frequency switching. The model demonstrates that transitions between slow and fast oscillations persist even when all neurons have identical time constants (C41), indicating connectivity is the primary determinant. Systematic variation of time constants shows they modulate the extent but not the presence of frequency switching (Figure 5E-H). This is a novel finding that contrasts with previous models (C86) and is well-supported by systematic parameter exploration.

results.result: Layer-specific differences in firing rates and oscillation power between superficial and deep layers arise from specific anatomical connections: stronger excitation and disinhibition in deep layers and stronger inhibition in superficial layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C25 and C88 explain layer differences through anatomy. The model identifies three key asymmetric connections: PYRsup→PYRdeep, translaminar SST, and stronger PV-PV connections in deep layers (Figure 2A). Selective removal of these connections abolishes layer differences in firing rates and oscillation power (Figure 2B-D). This is a well-controlled computational lesion study that establishes causal relationships between specific connections and observed layer differences.

results.result: Driving SST cells causes monotonic suppression of other cell types and reduces oscillation frequency, with oscillation power initially increasing then decreasing, replicating experimental surround suppression effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 describe SST-mediated inhibition. The model shows SST input monotonically suppresses PYR, PV, and VIP cells (C43, Figure 6B) and reduces oscillation frequency (C44). Oscillation power shows a non-monotonic response—initially increasing then decreasing as PV cells are suppressed (C45). This matches experimental observations of surround suppression in mouse V1 (C46, citations to Chen 2017, Veit et al. 2017), providing validation against independent data.

results.result: Strong pyramidal cell drive increases SST activity and can reverse the circuit from a disinhibited state back to an inhibited state, providing a homeostatic mechanism against runaway excitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C48, C49, and C104 describe PYR-mediated homeostasis. The model shows PYR input strongly increases SST activity (C47, Figure 7A). When the circuit is in a disinhibited state (VIP or PV active), sufficiently strong PYR input causes a sudden jump back to high SST activity (C48, C104), restoring inhibition. This matches optogenetic experiments showing high SST activity with strong PYR drive (C49, Hakim et al. 2018). The mechanism provides a plausible homeostatic control against excessive disinhibition.

results.result: Both feedforward (visual stimulation) and feedback (attention) input suppress low-frequency oscillations and enhance high-frequency oscillations through PV and VIP activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C57, and C89 describe responses to physiological input patterns. The model shows both feedforward (L4→L2/3) and feedback (ACC→VIP) input patterns suppress spontaneous low-frequency oscillations and enhance gamma oscillations (C56, Figure 9D). This matches experimental observations of alpha suppression and gamma enhancement during visual stimulation and attention (C57, C89, citations to van Kerkoerle et al. 2014, Klimesch 2012). The model successfully replicates multiple experimental phenomena.

results.result: The relative dominance of PV versus SST cell activity determines oscillation frequency and power, which are inversely related in the intact circuit but positively correlated when either cell type is silenced.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C26-C28, and C92 describe the relationship between interneuron activity and oscillations. The model shows PV knockout produces slow oscillations (~30 Hz) with high power, while SST knockout produces fast oscillations (~110 Hz) with low power (C26-C28). In the intact circuit, frequency and power are inversely related, but this relationship becomes positive when PV or SST cells are silenced (C29, C92). This provides insight into how different interneuron types control oscillatory dynamics.

results.result: The switching dynamics is preserved even without recurrent excitation among pyramidal cells, demonstrating that the switch is implemented by interactions among the three inhibitory neuron types.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 demonstrates the sufficiency of inhibitory interactions. The model shows that removing recurrent PYR-PYR connections does not abolish switching dynamics (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B), though it does affect oscillation frequency. This computational manipulation provides strong evidence that the switch mechanism is fundamentally implemented by inhibitory circuitry rather than requiring recurrent excitation, which is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: The switching dynamics is robust to noise and variability in connection weights, though weight variability affects the slope of response curves and Hill coefficient values.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C39 assess model robustness. Adding Gaussian noise does not change switching results (C38, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Jittering connection weights according to experimental variability changes response curve slopes and produces a range of Hill coefficients (C39, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C), but switching behavior persists. This demonstrates the mechanism is robust to biological variability, supporting its plausibility.

results.result: At high coupling parameter G values, feedforward and feedback input suppress SST and PYR activity, which is inconsistent with experimental observations, suggesting smaller G values may be more biologically realistic for mouse V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C98 and C99 identify a model limitation. The model shows SST and PYR suppression at high G values (C98), which contradicts experiments showing all cell types increase with visual stimulation (citations to Dipoppa et al. 2018, Kirchberger et al. 2021). The authors appropriately acknowledge this inconsistency and suggest smaller G values may be more realistic (C99). This is an honest assessment of model limitations and provides guidance for parameter selection.

results.result: The model is based on connectivity data from Jiang et al. 2015 that did not include layers 4 and 6, and there is limited anatomical knowledge about cell-specific connectivity in these layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C100 and C101 describe model limitations. The connectivity matrix is based on Jiang et al. 2015, which excluded layers 4 and 6 (C100). While cell types in these layers have been characterized, detailed connectivity information is lacking (C101, citations to Scala et al. 2019, Frandolig et al. 2019, etc.). This is an appropriate acknowledgment of the model's scope and limitations based on available data.

results.result: The model replicates experimental findings from monkey V1, including layer-specific oscillation patterns and stimulus size-dependent frequency transitions, suggesting canonical microcircuit principles may be shared across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 extend the model to monkey data. The model replicates some monkey V1 findings including gamma in superficial layers, slow oscillations in deep layers, and frequency transitions with stimulus size (C106, C107, citations to van Kerkoerle et al. 2014, Gieselmann and Thiele 2008). However, the inference that both species share common principles (C108) is speculative given the lack of detailed cell-type connectivity data in monkeys (citation to Vanni et al. 2021). The model is based on mouse data, so cross-species generalization requires additional validation.

results.result: The model makes testable predictions including: (1) asymmetric frequency-power changes are abolished with PV/SST silencing, (2) PYR drive produces linear or nonlinear inhibitory responses depending on circuit state, and (3) single-layer inhibitory cell stimulation propagates to the opposite layer.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 present testable predictions. These predictions follow logically from the model results: C109 from the silencing experiments (C92), C110 from the PYR input experiments (C47-C48), and C111 from the translaminar propagation experiments (C51-C52). The predictions are specific, experimentally feasible, and would provide strong tests of the model's mechanisms. This represents good scientific practice in computational modeling.

results.result: The computational model consists of two layers (L2/3 and L5) with four cell types each (PYR, PV, SST, VIP), using connectivity data from Jiang et al. 2015 corrected for cell type prevalence and scaled by a global coupling parameter G.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 and C117-C124 describe the model architecture and construction. The model is based on comprehensive experimental connectivity data from Jiang et al. 2015 (C118-C120), which was processed to create a single connectivity matrix (C121) and corrected for cell prevalence (C123-C124). VIP cells were divided into superficial and deep targeting types based on connectivity patterns (C122). The methodology is clearly described and appropriately references the source data. The scaling parameter G is justified by prior modeling work (C18, citations to Deco et al. 2013, Jobst et al. 2017).

results.result: Spontaneous activity in the model shows layer-specific patterns: higher firing rates in deep layers for PYR and SST cells, oscillation frequencies that decrease with increasing G, and layer-specific oscillation power distributions matching experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe spontaneous model behavior. The model shows PYR, PV, and VIP rates increase then decrease with G (C19), with SST showing slower dynamics (C20). Deep layer PYR and SST rates are higher, matching mouse experiments (C21, citations to Sakata and Harris 2009, Senzai et al. 2019). Oscillation frequency decreases from high gamma to beta/low gamma with increasing G (C22), remains higher in deep layers (C23), and shows layer-specific power distributions matching experiments (C24). These results validate the model against multiple experimental observations.

results.result: Pyramidal cell firing rates in each layer were used as a proxy for local field potentials (LFPs) in the model.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 describes a methodological choice. Using pyramidal cell rates as LFP proxies is a common simplification in rate models, but it is an approximation. True LFPs reflect weighted sums of synaptic currents across populations, not just pyramidal cell firing rates. While this approximation may capture some oscillatory dynamics, it may not accurately represent all aspects of LFP signals, particularly phase relationships and contributions from inhibitory neurons. The authors do not discuss the limitations of this approximation.

results.result: Bistability based on mutual inhibitory connections provides an alternative mechanism to recurrent excitation for persistent state transitions underlying working memory, attention, consciousness, and language processing, with anatomical heterogeneity potentially reflecting regional differences in switch types.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 propose broad implications. While the model demonstrates inhibition-based bistability as an alternative to excitation-based mechanisms (C76), the extension to working memory, attention, consciousness, and language is speculative. The model is of mouse V1 and does not directly address these cognitive functions. The suggestion that anatomical gradients reflect different switch types (C77) is an interesting hypothesis but lacks direct evidence. These claims represent reasonable speculation but require substantial additional work to validate.

results.result: Background claims establish the context: neocortical organization, interneuron classification, canonical microcircuits, disinhibition, oscillations, and gaps in understanding multilayer dynamics and rate-oscillation relationships.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C12 provide background context. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to established literature (Tremblay et al. 2016, Pfeffer et al. 2013, Jiang et al. 2015, Douglas and Martin 2004, Cardin et al. 2009, etc.). Claims C10 and C11 appropriately identify gaps in the literature that motivate the current study. This background is accurate and appropriately cited.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualize findings: SST cells as 'master regulators' in inhibited states, PV cells balancing excitation in disinhibited states, prior evidence for disinhibition, and evolutionary conservation of double negative feedback switches.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C71 place results in broader context. The characterization of SST as 'master regulators' (C64) and PV as balancing excitation (C65) are supported by the model and cited experimental work. Prior evidence for disinhibition (C66) and PV self-inhibition effects (C67-C68) are appropriately cited. The evolutionary conservation of double negative feedback (C71) is well-established in other biological systems (citations to Ferrell and Ha 2014, Ferrell 2002, Tyson et al. 2003). These discussion points appropriately contextualize the findings.

results.result: Summary and implications: the microcircuit functions as a homeostatic switch controlled by inhibitory neurons, with feedforward/feedback/lateral input regulating the switch position, providing an anatomically-based taxonomy for oscillations and mechanistic insight into oscillation function.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C90, C112-C116 summarize key findings and implications. The characterization of the microcircuit as a homeostatic switch (C112-C113) is well-supported by the modeling results. The suggestion that different inputs regulate switch position (C114) follows from the feedforward/feedback simulations. The proposed anatomical taxonomy for oscillations (C90) and mechanistic insights into oscillation function (C116) are reasonable inferences from the results, appropriately cited to relevant literature (Hahn et al. 2021, Klimesch et al. 2007, etc.).

results.result: The disinhibited state risks runaway excitation, but the microcircuit contains homeostatic mechanisms where strong pyramidal drive can reverse SST neurons to high firing rates, restoring inhibition, as observed experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C103, and C105 describe homeostatic control. The inference that disinhibition risks runaway excitation (C102) is reasonable. The model demonstrates that strong PYR drive can reverse SST suppression (C103, C104), providing homeostasis. This phenomenon has been observed experimentally (C105, citations to Pakan et al. 2016, Garcia Del Molino et al. 2017). This represents a plausible homeostatic mechanism supported by both modeling and experimental evidence.

results.result: Conduction delays were not modeled explicitly because distances within the microcircuit are very short.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 describes a modeling decision. The justification that conduction delays are negligible for short distances within a microcircuit is reasonable for a rate model operating at the timescales studied (tens to hundreds of milliseconds). However, for fast oscillations (gamma range, ~10 ms periods), even short delays could be relevant. The authors do not discuss whether this simplification might affect high-frequency oscillation dynamics.

results.result: Methodological definitions: ultrasensitivity is quantified using the Hill equation with Hill coefficient n>1 indicating sigmoidal responses; hysteresis indicates memory with non-collapsing response curves for increasing versus decreasing input.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 define analytical methods. The use of the Hill equation to quantify ultrasensitivity is standard and appropriately cited (Ferrell and Ha 2014). The definitions of Hill coefficient interpretation (C133) and hysteresis (C134-C135) are correct and standard in the field. These methodological approaches are appropriate for characterizing the switching dynamics.

results.result: The finding that connectivity pattern determines oscillation frequency provides a potential explanation for what determines oscillation frequency in neuronal circuits, contrasting with previous models that used different time constants.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C86 position the findings relative to prior work. The model's demonstration that connectivity determines frequency switching (C82-C84) does provide insight into oscillation frequency determination, appropriately cited to relevant questions in the field (Brunel and Wang 2003, Jia et al. 2013). The contrast with previous models using time constants (C86, citations to Hyafil et al. 2015, Mejias et al. 2016) is accurate. However, the claim of providing an 'explanation' may be overstated—the model provides one mechanism but doesn't exclude other mechanisms.

results.result: Experimental observations show layer-specific oscillation power, stimulus size-dependent frequency transitions mediated by lateral SST input, and the model suggests surround suppression switches the circuit from PV/VIP to SST dominated states.
results.evaluation: Claims C87, C93-C96 connect model results to experimental phenomena. Layer-specific oscillation power (C87) and stimulus size effects (C93) are well-documented experimentally (multiple citations). The anatomical basis for surround suppression via lateral SST input (C94, Adesnik et al. 2012) is established. The model's mechanistic interpretation (C95) is a reasonable inference that connects anatomy to function. The note about inverse effects (C96, Ray and Maunsell 2010) appropriately acknowledges complexity in experimental observations.

results.result: The coupling parameter G can be related to the overall cell count in the studied circuits.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 interprets the coupling parameter. The statement is supported by citation to previous work (Deco et al. 2013) that used similar scaling approaches. The interpretation is reasonable since G scales all connections proportionally, which approximates the effect of having more neurons. However, this is a simplification—real changes in cell count would also affect other properties like spatial extent and connection probability. The authors appropriately note this is a loose relationship.

results.result: Layer 4 preferentially drives PYR and PV cells in superficial layers, while feedback from anterior cingulate cortex mostly targets VIP cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C54 describe input patterns used in the model. These are based on experimental studies (citations to Adesnik et al. 2012 and Zhang et al. 2014) and are used to model feedforward and feedback input patterns. The claims accurately represent the cited experimental findings and provide appropriate biological grounding for the model simulations.

results.result: Inhibition-based ultrasensitivity and hysteresis commonly require strong inhibitory interactions between system components.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 states a general principle about ultrasensitivity and hysteresis. This is well-established in the systems biology literature and appropriately cited (Ferrell 2002). The principle is correctly applied to interpret the model results showing that increasing mutual inhibitory weights produces ultrasensitivity and hysteresis (C36).
